report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is only *partly* supported. CLA supplements may produce a **small reduction in total fat mass** in some adults, but evidence that they reliably reduce **abdominal/visceral fat** is limited and not strong enough to treat CLA as an effective belly-fat treatment.

The most directly relevant trial was a short (4-week) randomized study in obese middle-aged men with metabolic-syndrome features. It found CLA *may* reduce abdominal fat, but did **not** reduce overall obesity or improve other cardiovascular risk factors; the authors explicitly note the small sample and need for further study.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11477497/

A recent systematic review/meta-analysis of adult randomized trials assessed body mass, BMI, waist circumference, fat mass, body-fat percentage, and fat-free mass—more informative than one small trial. It supports evaluating CLA’s effects across body-composition outcomes, but does not establish a large, clinically meaningful, or specifically abdominal-fat effect.  
https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/british-journal-of-nutrition/article/effects-of-conjugated-linoleic-acid-supplementation-on-anthropometrics-and-body-composition-indices-in-adults-a-systematic-review-and-doseresponse-metaanalysis/A3F12F07BB3118D4F757D901C6E1E366

Earlier human meta-analysis found CLA’s fat-mass effects inconsistent across studies, despite clearer effects in animals.  
https://ajcn.nutrition.org/article/S0002-9165(23)28055-7/fulltext

Safety also warrants caution: a newer meta-analysis examined glycemic control and liver enzymes in people at cardiovascular risk, reflecting concerns that CLA’s metabolic effects are not uniformly beneficial.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10552395/

**Bottom line:** CLA is not well supported as a dependable way to reduce abdominal fat. Any benefit is likely modest, variable by CLA isomer/dose/person, and should not replace sustained dietary, activity, sleep, and medical weight-management strategies.
